Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- British Airways is asking thousands of its staff to work for free for up to four weeks, spokeswoman Kirsten Millard said Tuesday. British Airways plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. In an e-mail to all its staff, the airline offered workers between one and four weeks of unpaid leave -- but with the option to work during this period. British Airways employs just more than 40,000 people in the United Kingdom. Last month, the company posted a record annual loss of £400 million ($656 million). Its chief executive declared at the time there were "absolutely no signs of recovery" in the industry. "In 30 years in this business and I've never seen anything like this. This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced," said Willie Walsh, British Airways' chief executive.  Watch more about BA's request » . A spokesman for one of Britain's biggest unions said its workers could not afford to work for free for a month. "It's all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he's prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year," said Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite. He pointed out that the airline was not ordering staff to work without pay. "It's a request -- you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave." Demand for the airline's passenger seats and cargo holds fell during the last financial year, while its fuel bill rocketed to almost £3 billion ($4.7 billion). Walsh said British Airways' woes were inextricably linked to the downturn in the global economy and that there had been no sign of any "green shoots" of recovery. Like its premium-class competitors, British Airways is losing customers to cheaper rivals. The airline's premium passenger numbers fell 13 percent in the second half of last year, in line with the industry average. Total traffic fell 3.4 percent and while the airline carried 33.1 million passengers last year, it was a drop of 4.3 percent from the previous year. The dip in demand for British Airways' flights has forced a switch in strategy at the airline. From the end of last year, it has been trying to tempt passengers with lower fares, sacrificing profit per seat for "bums on seats." It plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. CNN's Alysen Miller contributed to this report.

# British Airways Slashes Capacity, Appeals to Staff for Unpaid Shifts Amid Deepening Aviation Crisis

*Carrier faces mounting pressure as operational challenges and cost concerns reshape the industry*

---

**LONDON** — British Airways is confronting one of the most turbulent periods in its recent history, announcing significant capacity reductions while simultaneously making the extraordinary appeal to some employees to consider working additional shifts on a voluntary or unpaid basis to help the carrier navigate acute operational strain.

## Capacity Cuts Take Hold

The flag carrier has been forced to trim thousands of flights from its schedule, affecting routes across its short-haul network in particular. The reductions come as the airline grapples with a combination of staffing shortages, supply chain constraints, and lingering aftershocks from the pandemic-era workforce contraction.

Industry analysts note that the capacity pullback represents a strategic retreat aimed at protecting the reliability of remaining services. By operating fewer flights, the airline hopes to reduce the cascade of cancellations and delays that have frustrated travelers and damaged the brand's reputation.

"When you're stretched too thin, running a leaner but more dependable schedule can actually be the responsible choice," said one aviation consultant. "The alternative — mass day-of-cancellations — is far more damaging to customer trust."

## The Controversial Appeal to Workers

Perhaps the most contentious development has been reports that management appealed to certain staff, including office-based and management personnel with relevant training, to volunteer for frontline duties during peak periods.

The move has drawn sharp criticism from trade unions, who argue that asking employees to contribute additional labor without appropriate compensation reflects deeper structural problems within the business.

Union representatives have characterized such appeals as symptomatic of years of aggressive cost-cutting that left the airline without adequate staffing buffers to absorb demand surges.

"You cannot cut your workforce to the bone and then expect goodwill to fill the gaps," a union spokesperson stated. "Our members deserve fair pay for the hours they work."

## Roots of the Crisis

The current predicament traces back to decisions made during the depths of the pandemic, when passenger demand evaporated and airlines shed tens of thousands of jobs to survive. British Airways parent company IAG implemented substantial redundancies during this period.

When travel demand rebounded faster and more forcefully than many carriers anticipated, the industry found itself unable to rehire and retrain staff quickly enough. Security screening, ground handling, cabin crew, and pilot positions all faced shortfalls.

Compounding these labor challenges, aircraft manufacturers and engine makers have struggled with their own supply chain difficulties, leaving some planned deliveries delayed and maintenance turnaround times extended.

## Financial and Competitive Pressures

The operational challenges arrive against a backdrop of rising costs. Elevated fuel prices, wage inflation, and increased regulatory compliance expenses have squeezed margins across the sector.

Meanwhile, budget competitors continue to expand aggressively, intensifying pressure on legacy carriers to control costs while maintaining service standards that justify their premium positioning.

For British Airways specifically, the situation poses reputational risks in the crucial premium and business-travel segments, where reliability and service quality command loyalty and higher fares.

## Industry-Wide Implications

British Airways is far from alone. Carriers across Europe and beyond have implemented similar capacity adjustments and issued warnings about summer operations. Major hubs have imposed passenger caps to prevent the chaotic scenes of overcrowded terminals and stranded travelers seen during previous peak seasons.

Aviation authorities and airport operators have entered into complex negotiations with airlines over how to manage demand within existing capacity constraints.

## Looking Ahead

As the airline works to stabilize its operations, questions remain about how quickly the carrier can rebuild its workforce and restore full scheduling. Recruitment and training pipelines take months to yield fully operational staff, suggesting that constraints may persist through coming seasons.

For passengers, the near-term outlook includes continued advice to arrive early, monitor flight status closely, and prepare for potential disruptions.

For British Airways management, the challenge lies in balancing cost discipline against the operational resilience needed to compete — all while maintaining the confidence of both a frustrated workforce and a demanding customer base.

The coming months will test whether the carrier's strategic adjustments prove sufficient to weather one of the most challenging operating environments the aviation industry has faced in decades.

---

# British Airways Faces Turbulence as Financial Pressures Mount

*By CNN Staff*

British Airways is confronting significant financial headwinds, prompting the flag carrier to consider grounding portions of its fleet as it seeks to weather ongoing economic challenges, according to industry sources.

## A Carrier Under Pressure

The airline, one of the crown jewels of International Airlines Group (IAG), has been navigating a difficult operating environment marked by rising costs, fluctuating demand, and intensifying competition from both budget rivals and Gulf carriers.

Industry analysts point to several factors weighing on the airline's balance sheet, including elevated fuel prices, wage pressures, and the substantial capital costs associated with maintaining a modern long-haul fleet.

"Legacy carriers like British Airways face a perfect storm of structural challenges," said one aviation analyst. "They carry higher cost bases than their low-cost competitors while trying to defend premium market share."

## The Plan to Park Aircraft

Central to the airline's response is a strategy to temporarily park aircraft during periods of weaker demand—a cost-management tool that allows carriers to reduce expenses tied to fuel, maintenance, and crewing.

Parking planes, however, is not without complications. Aircraft still incur storage and maintenance costs even when grounded, and reactivating them requires time and resources. The move also raises questions about route capacity and passenger convenience.

The airline has emphasized that any such measures would form part of a broader effort to align capacity with market conditions while protecting long-term competitiveness.

## Unions Sound the Alarm

The prospect of grounded aircraft has drawn sharp responses from labor unions, which fear the decisions could translate into reduced hours, hiring freezes, or job losses for the airline's workforce.

Union representatives have called for transparency and assurances that frontline staff will not bear the brunt of the airline's cost-cutting.

"Our members have already made significant sacrifices," a union spokesperson said. "We will not accept a situation where workers pay the price for decisions made in the boardroom."

Labor leaders are pressing management for detailed consultations, warning that unilateral action could inflame tensions at a carrier that has weathered industrial disputes in the past.

## Looking Ahead

British Airways maintains that it remains committed to its customers and its recovery trajectory, positioning current measures as prudent stewardship rather than retreat.

Still, the coming months are likely to test the relationship between management and labor, as well as the airline's ability to reassure investors and passengers alike.

For a carrier synonymous with British aviation heritage, the challenge now is charting a course back to stable skies.
